LD 1289 - An Act to Amend the Election Recount Process

Good morning Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs.
My name is Al Cleveland. l am here today as the Advocacy Director of the League of Women Voters of
Maine. The League is in support of LD 1289 with the proposed amendment.
We support reducing the threshold for recounts across the board and for "no deposit" recounts in
particular. The thresholds that we have been using in Maine are quite high relative to those in other statesl , particularly in the era when over 90% of our ballots are counted by scanners, which have proven
remarkably accurate.
We also support those provisions of the bill that permit the Office of the Secretary of State to include
sunk costs as well as incremental costs in what a losing candidate may be asked to pay when a
discretionary recount is unsuccessful.
The committee may wish to consider an amendment that would require the Secretary of State to set a
cap on the cost of any recount, particularly for legislative and single county races. The financial risk associated with a recount should not depend on particulars of the race which are outside of the candidate's control. For example, in the recent 2024 election, there were two ballot cards, which had to be sorted in order to recount legislative races. The sorting of ballot cards should not be billed to an unsuccessful recount candidate, nor should a candidate be charged more for a recount in House District 124 or 125, both of which are wholly contained within Scarborough, but for which the ballots would be
mixed, than a recount in District 102 which would require all of the Freeport ballots. We are not certain
to what degree the number of municipalities involved in a recount affects the time, and thus the cost, of a recount, but it seems unfair to charge more for a recount of House District 6, with ballots from 20 municipalities, than for a recount of House District 102, which would involve only the Freeport ballots.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify. We are happy to answer any questions.

Position:

SUPPORT

The Maine Town & City Clerks' Association is in support of LD 1289 and we thank you for the opportunity to outline our points for your committee.

Members felt that lowering the threshold percentage to trigger a required deposit could reduce the number of recount requests. In addition, allowing the Secretary of State to include payroll costs for state workers staffing the recount seems reasonable, since that is likely the highest cost in administering that process. Finally, municipalities who follow Title 21-A in administering local elections would like to be afforded the same benefits. It may add clarity to amend the language to remove the term "state" before "workers" on line 14, so that it clearly could also apply to municipal staff.

The Maine Town & City Clerks' Association appreciates the opportunity to share its testimony with the Committee. Should any questions arise, please feel free to contact me at (207)680-4210 or by email: pdubois@waterville-me.gov .

Testimony of Shenna Bellows, Secretary of State Department of the Secretary of State

April 7, 2025

Testifying in favor of
L.D. 1289 "An Act to Amend the Election Recount Process"

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans
and Legal Affairs, my name is Shenna Bellows, I live in Manchester, and I am the Secretary of State. I
am testifying in favor of L.D. 1289.
I have long said that Maine's elections are safe, secure, and accurate. Last November's General Election provided an excellent opportunity to demonstrate that last point when a record eleven legislative recounts were requested, along with a recount of the Second Congressional District.

The requested recounts ranged in apparent vote percentage difference from 0.0% to 7.1%. Of every recount that was conducted - two requests were withdrawn, which had apparent vote percentage
differences of 0.93% and 1.68% -- every recount verified the accuracy of the tabulators. The only post~ recount result which differed from the unofficial, preliminary result was House District 141, where an
apparent tie was found to be a one vote win for Representative Lanigan.

As we conducted more and more recounts throughout the month of November, it became clearer and
clearer to my team and me that the thresholds for what amount of deposit is required should be reigned
in. Recounts demand staff time and rental costs and must occur at a time when the Elections Division
staff are already busy with post-election work.

Only two of the eleven legislative recount requests required any deposit from the apparent losing candidate. For the one legislative recount above that threshold that was conducted, no further payment than the $2,500 deposit was required, despite about a dozen staff members spending a morning conducting a recount in a House race with an apparent 362 vote differential. This is not good
stewardship of state resources.

L.D. 1289 also makes clear in state law a candidate who requests a recount -- so a candidate who is an
apparent losing candidate -- and the result is not overturned, is responsible for paying the actual cost of the recount. In writing this testimony it became apparent that an additional clause on page l, line 32 is
necessary to specify that only candidates who must pay a deposit would be required to pay the cost of the recount. Our intent was that candidates whose unofficial results were close enough not to require a
deposit would not be required to pay for the cost of the recount. We offer this addition as a friendly
amendment. For deposits that are larger than the actual cost of conducting a recount, the excess will be returned to the requesting candidate, should the recount not overturn the result. L.D. 1289 does not change that if a recount does overturn a result, the deposit is returned to the requesting candidate. If the provisions in L.D. 1289 had been in place last fall, two more of the legislative races would have required deposits, and the state would have been reimbursed for the actual cost of the recount for the one that was conducted. (The other request was withdrawn.) Additionally, the state would have been reimbursed for the actual cost of conducting the Second Congressional District race, rather than the portion of the cost which had historically been charged. Thank you for the opportunity to provide this testimony, I encourage you to support L.D. 1289 with
this proposed amendment, and I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

Testimony of Senate Majority Leader Teresa S. Pierce introducing
LD 1289, An Act to Amend the Election Recount Process
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs April 7, 2025
Chair Hickman, Chair Supica, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans
and Legal Affairs, my name is Teresa S. Pierce. I serve as the Senate Majority Leader, representing
Senate District 25, which includes Falmouth, Cumberland, North Yarmouth, Yarmouth (majority),
Gray, and Long Island. Thank you for the opportunity to introduce LD 1289, An Act to Amend the
Election Recount Process.
Working with Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and the remarkable team at the Elections Division, I present this bill in an effort to support the Division by adjusting the threshold for taxpayer-funded recounts and liability for those costs, after costly and consuming recounts were requested following the 2024 elections. Secretary Bellows and her team, in accordance with state law, worked well into December on these recounts. The recounts are costly to taxpayers as they require secure space for the recount and unbudgeted payroll expenses in order to staff the recount. The bill before you seeks to amend the recount laws to provide greater clarity for candidates and ease the burden on taxpayers when a recount, within the qualifying margins, is requested.
Current Maine law doesn't require recounts but grants apparent losing candidates the ability to request one. Candidates do not have to pay a deposit on the recount if the statewide or multicounty
race is 1% or less of the election night margin of victory, or 1,000 votes, whichever is less, or 1.5%
for a legislative or single county office. As drafted, this bill would reduce by half the amount of votes in an election used to determine if a recount deposit is required. It would also clarify that the
candidate requesting the recount is required to pay the payroll costs of the state workers necessary to conduct the recount, in the actual cost of the recount.
Secretary Bellows will present a small technical amendment to clarify that in legislative and single county recounts, the actual cost of the recount will only be required to be paid when a deposit is required for the recount. I support that amendment.
Finally, this bill requires a refund be provided to the requesting candidate if the deposit paid is greater than the actual cost of the recount and requires the requesting candidate to pay the difference if the actual cost of the recount is more than the deposit paid.
Secretary Bellows and her team are here to speak to this bill in greater depth and provide additional
information as the subject matter experts. Thank you for the opportunity to present this bill, I'm happy to answer questions you may have.
